sessions.teaser: The group applied root cause analysis through peer challenges, a guest talk, and a collaborative chess debrief. Strong ambassadors carried the session.
sessions.fullSummary:
SECTION 1 — OVERVIEW
Meeting Objective: The Expo Session covering Chapter 22 (Root Cause Analysis) brought together ambassadors and members across Bali, Vietnam, and Singapore to practice applying root cause analysis through structured weekly challenges, a guest speaker talk, and a chess-based interactive activity. The session aimed to deepen both conceptual understanding and real-world application of the methodology.
Total Meeting Duration: 2 hours 0 minutes 5 seconds
Host / Facilitator: BLCOP (Session Host, Ambassador); ELF 001 (Co-host, Program Coordinator); MIHF (Activity Facilitator); DAV79 (Senior Program Leader, strategic interventions); SAHN (Guest Observer / Breathing Exercise Advisor)
Participant Roles:
- I Putu Ratama — Guest Speaker, teacher at SMKN1 Bali Tourism High School
- Giani — Ambassador, Bali; Weekly Challenge Presenter
- Kyla — Ambassador, Bali/Yogyakarta; Weekly Challenge Presenter
- JFP (Jeffrey) — Ambassador; Weekly Challenge Presenter
- Ali (Alwe) — Ambassador; Weekly Challenge Presenter
- Mike-Nguyen Huu Manh — Participant, Vietnam team
- Luna the fox — Participant, Vietnam team (joined from restaurant)
- Ben — Participant, Vietnam team (difficult to reach)
- Ratna — Member, Bali; led breathing exercise
- Izzar — Member; active in chess activity
- Hana — Member, Vietnam; minimal verbal engagement
- Wyati — Member, Bali; connectivity issues
Overall Engagement Level: Medium
Overall Sentiment: Mixed — core ambassadors drove positive energy through strong challenge presentations, while newer and Vietnam members remained largely passive or disengaged for much of the session.
Notable Dynamics: A pronounced two-tier engagement gap defined the session — BLCOP, Giani, Kyla, JFP, and MIHF drove virtually all substantive content while the majority of newer members (Hana, Ben, Wyati, Ratna) could not formulate questions or contribute meaningfully when called upon. DAV79's early accountability-focused intervention set a firm but motivating tone.
Session Effectiveness Score: 6.5/10 — Giani's challenge and MIHF's chess activity were genuine highlights that elevated the session's learning quality, and DAV79's strategic framework provided useful structure for the next six months. However, persistent participation gaps among newer members, a weak challenge from Ali, early topic confusion from ELF, and time pressure in the final stretch held the session below its potential.
---
SECTION 2 — KEY DISCUSSIONS & TOPICS
Scoreboard Review and Accountability (Chapter 21: Pattern Recognition)
BLCOP opened with a detailed walk-through of last week's scoreboard from the pattern recognition session, covering individual scores and the group's emotional landscape. JFP led with 7.1, followed by Kailav at 6.8, ELF at 6.4, Jaden at 5.4, Ali at 5.1, Izzar and Giani at 4.7, Ratna at 3.9, and Intan at 2.0. The group's emotional distribution showed 43% positive, 50% neutral, and 7% mixed — with no negative emotions registered.

Key discussion points:
BLCOP flagged a decline in question volume and quality, noting that many questions were repetitive surface-level prompts such as "what gave you that idea?" or "what did you learn?" — the kind that yield low scores. He emphasized that higher-scoring questions build on previous answers or open up new lines of inquiry. Giani, Jaden, and Intan had not completed their challenges from the previous week, which BLCOP called out explicitly.

Insights or decisions:
DAV79 intervened with a critical reframe: scoreboards should not be read as dry data but as a mirror of mindset progress. He challenged BLCOP and the group to add energy, context, and narrative to scoreboard recaps — even a simple number like a score should be made exciting. He also noted that almost no one was writing notes on Substack after sessions, calling this out as a direct failure of follow-through that would limit learning retention.

Questions addressed:
DAV79 directed a live recall question to Kyla, asking her to name the most impactful question she had encountered in the previous session. Kyla attributed it to Jayden, who had asked about the root of her habits. DAV79 used this moment to model how to add contextual depth to session recaps — a teaching-through-example approach.

---
6-Month Work Plan and Ambassador Accountability Framework
DAV79 took over the screen to walk through the team's rotating session leadership plan spanning the next six months. A structured assignment list showed members committed to specific roles — speaker, writer, or content provider — for each session date through June and July, with the expectation that all roles would be fulfilled on time.

Key discussion points:
DAV79 explained the ambassador point system: completing commitments on time across two quarters could yield 280–400 points, sufficient to retain ambassador status above the 300-point threshold. Missing or late submissions result in negative scoring, and any member whose total drops below 300 will have to pay to attend future bootcamps. JFP was specifically flagged for submitting materials three days late, earning a red flag in the system. Members wishing to take on more assignments for additional points could request additions through a form DAV79 would share. Kyla was given a direct challenge: arrange for her mother to speak at next week's session.

Insights or decisions:
Giani was assigned the coordination role for all Bali members — Wyati, Sekar, Intan, Ratna, and others — with the explicit task of ensuring they complete their readings, registrations, and challenges. DAV79 framed forgetting as a mindset problem: "not caring is a mindset, and that is really, really bad."

---
Breathing Exercise (Led by Ratna, Feedback from SAHN)
BLCOP called on members to volunteer for the session-opening breathing exercise, initially attempting Wyati from Bali. Wyati's audio was inaudible despite multiple prompts, and DAV79 escalated by warning that non-responsiveness carries score penalties. BLCOP then moved to Ratna, who also struggled with the format initially. Giani provided a quick Indonesian translation and a live demonstration of the count-and-hold pattern to help Ratna calibrate.

Key discussion points:
Ratna completed a passable second attempt — inhale for 5 counts, hold for 3, exhale for 5 — and was thanked by BLCOP. SAHN, who had joined mid-exercise, provided detailed developmental feedback: the objective of the exercise is to energize and focus, not to induce calm sleepiness, and the person leading it must themselves feel relaxed and project energy. He recommended at least 5–6 repetitions with deliberate pacing.

Insights or decisions:
The breathing exercise continues to expose a readiness gap among newer Bali members. The repeated need for emergency demos and escalation from DAV79 suggests this format needs clearer pre-briefing for participants unfamiliar with the routine.

---
Guest Speaker: I Putu Ratama on Root Cause Analysis and the Growth Mindset
I Putu Ratama, a teacher at SMKN1 Bali (described as one of Bali's largest tourism vocational schools and a strong supporter of the Global Citizen Program), delivered an approximately 15-minute talk invited by DAV79 on short notice.

Key discussion points:
Mr. Ratama opened by reframing root cause analysis not purely as a problem-solving tool but as a daily practice of curiosity — asking questions about one's own strategies and life purpose. He drew on Carol Dweck's Mindset to contrast fixed mindset (passive, accepting whatever happens, not questioning) with growth mindset (adaptive, strategy-interrogating, always asking why). He argued that people with fixed mindsets stop questioning and simply live by default, whereas growth-minded individuals continuously examine whether their current strategies are aligned with their goals. He also connected mental resilience — the capacity to survive adversity and adapt under pressure — as a prerequisite for effective root cause thinking.

Insights or decisions:
DAV79 praised the talk for its well-timed and well-suited content, noting the growth mindset framing was a natural complement to the session's academic focus. Mr. Ratama was invited to stay for questions and remained for a portion of the challenge segment before departing.

---
Weekly Challenge Presentations
The session's substantive core featured four ambassador presentations applying root cause analysis to real or observed personal stories.

Giani's Challenge — RCA of Kyla's Cooking Competition Experience
Giani presented a third-party root cause analysis of Kyla's experience during a cooking competition, where Kyla felt that teammates were ignoring her suggestions because they kept explaining things she already knew. Through a structured sequence of why-questions and direct interviews with Kyla, Giani traced the surface frustration (feeling underestimated) back to a deeper root: a mismatch between Kyla's expectation of collaborative recognition and the team's efficiency-first working style under time pressure. The teammates were not excluding her — they were simply prioritizing task completion. Kyla's inability to immediately resolve the situation was traced further to her preference for following a leader rather than asserting herself in ambiguous, high-speed environments.

Insights or decisions:
DAV79 praised Giani's challenge as the first time he had observed an ambassador apply genuine third-party observational depth to connect a real-life social experience back to an academic framework. He specifically praised BLCOP's follow-up question — asking Giani to articulate the explicit connection to root cause analysis — as one of the best questions he had seen in the program.

---
Kyla's Challenge — 5 Whys Applied to Giani's Graduation Photo Frustration
Kyla applied the 5 Whys technique to Giani's real frustration: Giani's mother had submitted an AI-generated photo of Giani to the graduation yearbook without permission. Kyla's five-question sequence began with Giani's surface anger at her mother, then traced through aesthetic embarrassment (the AI background looked unnatural), the mother's intent to match a theme, the lack of a prior conversation about preferences, and finally the root cause: the absence of consent, open communication, and the permanent nature of the decision once sent.

Insights or decisions:
Luna asked a thoughtful question about what tips Kyla would offer to help Giani feel better, and Giani followed up by asking what Kyla herself would have done in her position. Kyla's answer — talk it out, try to have the photo changed, and if not, practice acceptance — showed practical resolution thinking. Wyati contributed a written chat thought, sharing she had faced a similar situation and chosen to retake her photo before printing.

---
JFP's Challenge — RCA of a Forgotten Art Assessment
JFP presented a personal 3-Why analysis: he had forgotten to bring a weighted art assessment worksheet to school, initially attributing it to being in a hurry. Tracing deeper, he found he had rushed because he was completing other homework the night before and forgot to pack his bag; and the deeper cause was procrastination — repeatedly delaying work until the last minute, which created a cascading time pressure that led to the oversight. JFP proposed a behavioral correction: setting timers for each assignment to impose structure and prevent future delays.

Insights or decisions:
Giani's written question — asking JFP to connect his experience to discipline and consistency — was the most analytically probing question of this segment, and JFP's response was lucid: the incident revealed a laid-back attitude that had gone too far. BLCOP noted that JFP's participation outside his own segment had been limited and encouraged more engagement.

---
Ali's Challenge — Root Cause Tracing of a Rocket-Building Skill
Ali presented a challenge tracing how he developed his current skills in rocket design within games, citing his observation of a star as an early spark of curiosity, followed by building ugly initial rockets and improving after watching a YouTuber. His stated goal is to eventually work with NASA designing rockets. The connection to root cause analysis was not explicitly structured within the presentation and had to be elicited verbally by BLCOP, who also noted that the challenge was embedded in the content rather than presented as a clear separate section.

Insights or decisions:
BLCOP gave constructive feedback: define the challenge explicitly on a dedicated slide, explain technical terms (he clarified the thrust-to-weight ratio formula for non-specialists), and integrate the why-question structure directly into the presentation content rather than responding to it only when prompted. JFP asked a strong follow-up: how does Ali plan to actually reach NASA — as a rocket builder, an astronaut, or otherwise — and how will root cause analysis support that path. Ali clarified his goal and linked RCA to fixing technical failures in his designs.

---
Chess Activity — Root Cause Analysis Through Collaborative Play
MIHF facilitated a group chess match against "Captain Rook" on chess.com, calling on individual participants one by one to suggest moves. The activity generated the highest energy of the session — participants were animated, debated moves in real time, and experienced both the thrill of capturing pieces and the frustration of falling into check repeatedly. The team lost their queen mid-game and ultimately could not recover before MIHF paused at the two-hour mark.

Key discussion points:
Participation was significantly broader than in the challenge Q&A segments: Izzar, Luna, Ali, Mike, Kyla, JFP, and BLCOP all contributed moves or coaching. Many had limited chess knowledge but embraced the collaborative uncertainty. MIHF connected the game to root cause analysis in the debrief: when the team lost their queen, the visible cause was that the queen was undefended — but the true root cause was a failure of board awareness, a lapse in seeing the whole picture. This was offered as a concrete analogy for how root cause analysis requires looking past the immediate problem to the underlying lapse in attention, strategy, or discipline that allowed it to happen.

Insights or decisions:
MIHF teased a potential continuation of the game next week, keeping the group motivated. The activity demonstrated that well-designed experiential learning can rapidly increase participation breadth even among typically passive members.

---
Session Wrap-Up and Next Week Preview
ELF closed with announcements for the following week. The topic will be Emotional Intelligence (Chapter 23). Ali will serve as host, ELF will serve as material provider, and Ratna was also assigned materials (though she was non-responsive at session close and DAV79 tasked Giani with texting her on WhatsApp). MIHF hinted that next week's activity would be even more engaging.

Key discussion points:
DAV79 appeared to have exited the call before ELF's closing remarks; ELF confirmed his absence and proceeded independently. All members were reminded to read the chapters and submit comments. The session ended warmly with goodnight messages from Giani, Kyla, Izzar, and others.

---
SECTION 3 — CHAT BOX SUMMARY
The VTT transcript does not log chat box messages as separate entries, but multiple verbal references to chat activity throughout the session allow reconstruction of key exchanges.

Participant Questions via Chat During Challenge Segments
Ali contributed a written question to the chat during Giani's challenge, asking about Kyla's emotional journey from the beginning to the end of the cooking competition — initially addressing it to Giani but refining it to ask what she would have felt in Kyla's position. BLCOP read this aloud and facilitated the response verbally. Giani also submitted a written question to the chat during JFP's segment, asking whether JFP connected his experience to discipline and consistency — a notably analytical prompt that BLCOP read out and that JFP answered with clarity.

Wyati's Contribution During Kyla's Challenge
During Kyla's 5-Why presentation about the graduation photo, Wyati posted a written thought in the chat sharing that she had faced a similar graduation photo situation and had chosen to retake the photo before it was printed. BLCOP relayed this to Giani verbally and invited a response. Giani acknowledged Wyati's solution as a good one, but noted that in her case the photo had already been sent without her knowledge, which was the crux of the frustration. This was Wyati's sole substantive contribution given her connectivity limitations.

Chess Activity Chat as Real-Time Coaching
During the chess game, the chat box became an active real-time coaching space. Luna, Izzar, and Ali all posted suggested moves for participants who were currently "on turn" and struggling to decide. MIHF explicitly told Hannah to check the chat for help when she froze on her move. This represented a spontaneous peer-support dynamic where the chat functioned as a lower-pressure contribution channel for participants less confident speaking aloud.

Missed Opportunity
The chat remained significantly underused as a substantive engagement channel across the challenge presentations. Ben, Hana, and Izzar — all of whom struggled to formulate spoken questions — could have been more actively guided toward posting written questions or observations in the chat box. BLCOP made occasional prompts in this direction but did not systematically position the chat as the default fallback for quieter participants.

---
SECTION 4 — QUESTIONS BY PARTICIPANT

DAV79's Question to Kyla — Recalling the Most Impactful Question from Last Week
During the scoreboard review, DAV79 directly called on Kyla to identify the most impactful question from the previous pattern recognition session. The purpose was not mere recall — it was a live modeling exercise to show the group how to give meaningful context to scoreboard recaps. Kyla attributed the question to Jayden, who had asked about the root of her habits. DAV79 used this to push a broader point: even a scoreboard presentation should be treated as an opportunity to transmit insight, not just data. The question revealed DAV79's standard — that every session element, even administrative reviews, should add momentum and learning.

BLCOP's Question to Giani — Connecting the Challenge Explicitly to Root Cause Analysis
After Giani presented her analysis of Kyla's cooking competition story, BLCOP asked her to articulate the major connection between what she had prepared and the methodology of root cause analysis. The question was a precise facilitation move: Giani had demonstrated strong analytical instincts implicitly, but had not named the framework explicitly. BLCOP's challenge forced that naming. Giani's response — that she had interviewed Kyla, asked structured questions, and analyzed the experience to identify underlying rather than surface causes — validated the work. BLCOP added a refinement: following a single converging why-chain rather than separate branches would have produced a cleaner root cause structure. DAV79 praised this question as "sharp and cool" and among the best he had seen in the program.

Ali's Question to Giani — Perspective-Taking in the Cooking Competition
Ali read a question from the chat asking how the subject of the story — initially Kyla, then reframed as Giani herself — felt at the beginning and end of the situation. The question was somewhat confused in formulation, partly because Ali was reading a chat message while speaking aloud. Despite the awkward delivery, the question probed empathy and perspective-taking — asking the analyst to step into the subject's emotional experience rather than remaining in observer mode. Giani navigated it by distinguishing her role as external analyst from Kyla's role as subject, then offering a thoughtful reflection on what she would have done differently in Kyla's position.

Kyla's Role-Reversal Question to Giani — Handling the Competition Conflict
Kyla asked Giani directly: if she were in Kyla's position during the competition, how would she have handled the situation? This question tested whether Giani's analysis had yielded a practical resolution strategy. Giani's answer — that she would have clarified task assignments upfront to prevent the misunderstanding from arising — demonstrated that the root cause analysis had produced an actionable insight, not just a diagnosis. The question closed the loop between analytical process and behavioral outcome.

Luna's Question to Kyla — Attitude Change for Giani
Luna, joining from a restaurant with intermittent audio, asked Kyla whether she had any tips or attitude changes that could help Giani feel better about the graduation photo situation. Despite audio challenges, the question reached for something beyond diagnosis — it sought a constructive emotional resolution pathway. Kyla recommended that Giani talk out her frustrations rather than letting them build, and choose reconciliation over argument. Luna's question added an emotional intelligence dimension to what had been primarily an analytical exercise.

Giani's Question to Kyla — What Would You Do Instead of Arguing?
Giani turned the discussion back to Kyla with a direct role-reversal: what would Kyla actually do if she were in Giani's position, rather than arguing with her mother? Kyla's response was practical and emotionally mature — she would talk directly to her mother about why she disliked the photo, attempt to persuade the teacher to change it, and if that failed, practice acceptance and move on positively. This exchange completed a peer learning loop where the subject and the analyst each applied the other's perspective constructively.

JFP's Questions to Ali — Connecting Rocket-Building to Goals and RCA
JFP asked Ali two related questions. The first — a broad opener about how root cause analysis helps in daily life — was answered plainly by Ali. The second was more probing: given Ali's stated goal of working at NASA, what was his actual path — build rockets himself, become an astronaut, or something else? JFP also added a reflection that root cause analysis requires patience to trace a problem or goal back to its source. Ali clarified his goal is designing rockets at NASA and acknowledged that RCA would help him diagnose technical failures. JFP's engagement here was notably more reflective than his participation elsewhere in the session.

---

---
SECTION 7 — SESSION EFFECTIVENESS: STRENGTHS & IMPROVEMENTS
Strengths
- Giani's challenge set a new analytical standard for the program — applying third-party observation, structured why-questions, and empathetic insight, she produced the most depth-of-analysis the program had seen to date; DAV79's specific and public praise gave this moment genuine instructional weight for peers.
- MIHF's chess activity was the session's creative high point — well-designed to maximize broad participation, it generated authentic energy across skill levels and concluded with a crisp, memorable metaphor for root cause analysis that unified the session's learning theme.
- BLCOP maintained strong facilitation discipline throughout a 2-hour multi-segment session: he kept the structure intact, deployed sharp probing questions, and managed a geographically dispersed group with patience and consistency.
- DAV79's early work plan presentation was direct, consequential, and actionable — participants left with a clear understanding of the scoring system, the ambassador threshold, and their individual responsibilities for the next six months.
- The peer challenge exchanges between Giani and Kyla — where each applied the 5 Whys or structured analysis to the other's experience — created authentic co-learning rather than isolated presentations; this format should be repeated.
Areas for Improvement
- Ali's challenge was structurally incomplete and insufficiently connected to root cause analysis; the challenge itself was not identified as a separate section, technical terms were unexplained, and the methodology was only visible through verbal prompting by BLCOP — a pre-submission review checklist could prevent this.
- Newer and Vietnam participants (Hana, Ben, Ratna, Wyati) were unable to formulate questions or engage substantively when called upon, indicating insufficient onboarding into the questioning culture and format expectations of the Expo; a short pre-session briefing document for new members is worth considering.
- ELF's misidentification of the session topic at the opening ("pattern recognition" instead of "root cause analysis") was a visible preparation gap that required DAV79's correction — this should not occur for the co-host, and a pre-session topic check is a minimum standard.
- The breathing exercise transition consumed disproportionate time due to Wyati's audio failure and Ratna's initial uncertainty — if front-line members are not prepared, the exercise should be pre-assigned the day before rather than asked for on-the-spot volunteers.
- The session ran into time pressure in the final 30 minutes: BLCOP had to leave early, Ali's challenge was compressed, and MIHF combined the activity with the thought of the day; a hard cut-off protocol at 90 minutes for challenge presentations would preserve the closing quality.

---
SECTION 8 — ENGAGEMENT SCORE
DAV79: Score 8/10 — High-quality interventions on scoreboard philosophy, the 6-month work plan, and ambassador accountability; specific, motivating praise of Giani's challenge was a session highlight. Slight reduction for exiting before the formal close without transition acknowledgment.
BLCOP: Score 8/10 — Excellent host across a complex 2-hour session with sharp probing questions, patient participation management, and consistent structural control. Slight deduction for needing to exit early without securing a backup plan for the closing.
ELF 001: Score 5/10 — Delivered a clear wrap-up and demonstrated accountability by committing to send the evaluation the following day, but the early topic misidentification and limited engagement during challenge segments reduced the overall impact.
MIHF: Score 8/10 — The chess activity design and debrief were the session's most creative contribution. Strong inclusive energy management and a clear, well-executed conceptual payoff in the debrief connected the activity to the session's learning objective.
SAHN: Score 6/10 — Brief but substantive contribution on breathing exercise quality; his coaching on purpose, pacing, and repetitions was specific and actionable.
I Putu Ratama: Score 7/10 — Delivered a genuine and relatable talk grounding root cause analysis in classroom experience and Dweck's mindset framework; his real-world examples made the content accessible and the growth mindset framing was well-timed.
Giani: Score 9/10 — Outstanding challenge presentation using third-party perspective, structured questioning, and analytical depth; received the highest praise in the session from DAV79. Active as peer questioner and supporter throughout.
Kyla: Score 8/10 — Strong 5-Why analysis, active questioning across multiple challenge segments, and genuine peer generosity in role-reversal exchanges with Giani. Consistent contributor throughout the session.
JFP: Score 7/10 — Clean and self-aware personal challenge with a clear root cause and actionable solution; follow-up questions to Ali showed growth in critical thinking. BLCOP's note about limited general participation outside his own segment is a valid flag.
Ali: Score 5/10 — High energy in chess and Q&A phases, but the challenge presentation required significant facilitation support to uncover its connection to root cause analysis. Enthusiasm is a clear asset; preparation discipline needs to match it.
Mike-Nguyen Huu Manh: Score 4/10 — Present throughout but struggled to formulate questions verbally; chess contribution was the strongest visible moment. Needs scaffolding to engage more substantively in structured discussion formats.
Luna the fox: Score 5/10 — Environmental limitations reduced contribution quality, but she demonstrated genuine engagement in the chess activity and attempted a thoughtful question to Kyla. Joining from a noisy restaurant was a self-imposed limitation.
Izzar: Score 5/10 — Notably strong during the chess game with strategic real-time suggestions; quiet and hesitant in challenge Q&A phases. Written chat question to JFP about discipline and consistency was the best analytical contribution from this participant.
Ratna: Score 3/10 — Completed the breathing exercise after coaching but otherwise showed minimal verbal engagement and non-responsiveness at key moments. Connectivity and readiness concerns are ongoing.
Hana: Score 2/10 — Could not formulate a question or share a thought when directly called upon; single-word verbal responses throughout the session. Direct onboarding support is needed before the next session.
Ben: Score 2/10 — Difficult to reach across the session, no substantive contribution when eventually connected. Peer intervention was required simply to locate him — a participation commitment issue.
Wyati: Score 3/10 — Persistent connectivity issues limited participation significantly; a single written chat contribution during Kyla's challenge (about the graduation photo) was insightful but isolated.

Giani was assigned the coordination role for all Bali members — Wyati, Sekar, Intan, Ratna, and others — with the explicit task of ensuring they complete their readings, registrations, and challenges. DAV79 framed forgetting as a mindset problem: "not caring is a mindset, and that is really, really bad."

---
Breathing Exercise (Led by Ratna, Feedback from SAHN)
BLCOP called on members to volunteer for the session-opening breathing exercise, initially attempting Wyati from Bali. Wyati's audio was inaudible despite multiple prompts, and DAV79 escalated by warning that non-responsiveness carries score penalties. BLCOP then moved to Ratna, who also struggled with the format initially. Giani provided a quick Indonesian translation and a live demonstration of the count-and-hold pattern to help Ratna calibrate.

Key discussion points:
Ratna completed a passable second attempt — inhale for 5 counts, hold for 3, exhale for 5 — and was thanked by BLCOP. SAHN, who had joined mid-exercise, provided detailed developmental feedback: the objective of the exercise is to energize and focus, not to induce calm sleepiness, and the person leading it must themselves feel relaxed and project energy. He recommended at least 5–6 repetitions with deliberate pacing.

Insights or decisions:
The breathing exercise continues to expose a readiness gap among newer Bali members. The repeated need for emergency demos and escalation from DAV79 suggests this format needs clearer pre-briefing for participants unfamiliar with the routine.

---
Guest Speaker: I Putu Ratama on Root Cause Analysis and the Growth Mindset
I Putu Ratama, a teacher at SMKN1 Bali (described as one of Bali's largest tourism vocational schools and a strong supporter of the Global Citizen Program), delivered an approximately 15-minute talk invited by DAV79 on short notice.

Key discussion points:
Mr. Ratama opened by reframing root cause analysis not purely as a problem-solving tool but as a daily practice of curiosity — asking questions about one's own strategies and life purpose. He drew on Carol Dweck's Mindset to contrast fixed mindset (passive, accepting whatever happens, not questioning) with growth mindset (adaptive, strategy-interrogating, always asking why). He argued that people with fixed mindsets stop questioning and simply live by default, whereas growth-minded individuals continuously examine whether their current strategies are aligned with their goals. He also connected mental resilience — the capacity to survive adversity and adapt under pressure — as a prerequisite for effective root cause thinking.

Insights or decisions:
DAV79 praised the talk for its well-timed and well-suited content, noting the growth mindset framing was a natural complement to the session's academic focus. Mr. Ratama was invited to stay for questions and remained for a portion of the challenge segment before departing.

---
Weekly Challenge Presentations
The session's substantive core featured four ambassador presentations applying root cause analysis to real or observed personal stories.

Giani's Challenge — RCA of Kyla's Cooking Competition Experience
Giani presented a third-party root cause analysis of Kyla's experience during a cooking competition, where Kyla felt that teammates were ignoring her suggestions because they kept explaining things she already knew. Through a structured sequence of why-questions and direct interviews with Kyla, Giani traced the surface frustration (feeling underestimated) back to a deeper root: a mismatch between Kyla's expectation of collaborative recognition and the team's efficiency-first working style under time pressure. The teammates were not excluding her — they were simply prioritizing task completion. Kyla's inability to immediately resolve the situation was traced further to her preference for following a leader rather than asserting herself in ambiguous, high-speed environments.

Insights or decisions:
DAV79 praised Giani's challenge as the first time he had observed an ambassador apply genuine third-party observational depth to connect a real-life social experience back to an academic framework. He specifically praised BLCOP's follow-up question — asking Giani to articulate the explicit connection to root cause analysis — as one of the best questions he had seen in the program.

---
Kyla's Challenge — 5 Whys Applied to Giani's Graduation Photo Frustration
Kyla applied the 5 Whys technique to Giani's real frustration: Giani's mother had submitted an AI-generated photo of Giani to the graduation yearbook without permission. Kyla's five-question sequence began with Giani's surface anger at her mother, then traced through aesthetic embarrassment (the AI background looked unnatural), the mother's intent to match a theme, the lack of a prior conversation about preferences, and finally the root cause: the absence of consent, open communication, and the permanent nature of the decision once sent.

Insights or decisions:
Luna asked a thoughtful question about what tips Kyla would offer to help Giani feel better, and Giani followed up by asking what Kyla herself would have done in her position. Kyla's answer — talk it out, try to have the photo changed, and if not, practice acceptance — showed practical resolution thinking. Wyati contributed a written chat thought, sharing she had faced a similar situation and chosen to retake her photo before printing.

---
JFP's Challenge — RCA of a Forgotten Art Assessment
JFP presented a personal 3-Why analysis: he had forgotten to bring a weighted art assessment worksheet to school, initially attributing it to being in a hurry. Tracing deeper, he found he had rushed because he was completing other homework the night before and forgot to pack his bag; and the deeper cause was procrastination — repeatedly delaying work until the last minute, which created a cascading time pressure that led to the oversight. JFP proposed a behavioral correction: setting timers for each assignment to impose structure and prevent future delays.

Insights or decisions:
Giani's written question — asking JFP to connect his experience to discipline and consistency — was the most analytically probing question of this segment, and JFP's response was lucid: the incident revealed a laid-back attitude that had gone too far. BLCOP noted that JFP's participation outside his own segment had been limited and encouraged more engagement.

---
Ali's Challenge — Root Cause Tracing of a Rocket-Building Skill
Ali presented a challenge tracing how he developed his current skills in rocket design within games, citing his observation of a star as an early spark of curiosity, followed by building ugly initial rockets and improving after watching a YouTuber. His stated goal is to eventually work with NASA designing rockets. The connection to root cause analysis was not explicitly structured within the presentation and had to be elicited verbally by BLCOP, who also noted that the challenge was embedded in the content rather than presented as a clear separate section.

Insights or decisions:
BLCOP gave constructive feedback: define the challenge explicitly on a dedicated slide, explain technical terms (he clarified the thrust-to-weight ratio formula for non-specialists), and integrate the why-question structure directly into the presentation content rather than responding to it only when prompted. JFP asked a strong follow-up: how does Ali plan to actually reach NASA — as a rocket builder, an astronaut, or otherwise — and how will root cause analysis support that path. Ali clarified his goal and linked RCA to fixing technical failures in his designs.

---
Chess Activity — Root Cause Analysis Through Collaborative Play
MIHF facilitated a group chess match against "Captain Rook" on chess.com, calling on individual participants one by one to suggest moves. The activity generated the highest energy of the session — participants were animated, debated moves in real time, and experienced both the thrill of capturing pieces and the frustration of falling into check repeatedly. The team lost their queen mid-game and ultimately could not recover before MIHF paused at the two-hour mark.

Key discussion points:
Participation was significantly broader than in the challenge Q&A segments: Izzar, Luna, Ali, Mike, Kyla, JFP, and BLCOP all contributed moves or coaching. Many had limited chess knowledge but embraced the collaborative uncertainty. MIHF connected the game to root cause analysis in the debrief: when the team lost their queen, the visible cause was that the queen was undefended — but the true root cause was a failure of board awareness, a lapse in seeing the whole picture. This was offered as a concrete analogy for how root cause analysis requires looking past the immediate problem to the underlying lapse in attention, strategy, or discipline that allowed it to happen.

Insights or decisions:
MIHF teased a potential continuation of the game next week, keeping the group motivated. The activity demonstrated that well-designed experiential learning can rapidly increase participation breadth even among typically passive members.

---
Session Wrap-Up and Next Week Preview
ELF closed with announcements for the following week. The topic will be Emotional Intelligence (Chapter 23). Ali will serve as host, ELF will serve as material provider, and Ratna was also assigned materials (though she was non-responsive at session close and DAV79 tasked Giani with texting her on WhatsApp). MIHF hinted that next week's activity would be even more engaging.

DAV79 appeared to have exited the call before ELF's closing remarks; ELF confirmed his absence and proceeded independently. All members were reminded to read the chapters and submit comments. The session ended warmly with goodnight messages from Giani, Kyla, Izzar, and others.

Total Meeting Duration: 1 hour 27 minutes 24 seconds

Session Effectiveness Score: 6/10 — The session successfully delivered its core content including a mindfulness exercise, guest speaker talk, and member challenges, creating a well-rounded learning experience. However, technical difficulties, audio issues, low attendance, and unclear role assignments for upcoming duties reduced overall effectiveness.
---
SECTION 2 — KEY DISCUSSIONS & TOPICS
Program Performance Review & Scoreboard
The session opened with alwe sharing the screen to present a performance scoreboard for the ambassador program. The scoreboard displayed individual point tallies for each member, reflecting their cumulative contributions to the program. According to the data presented, Bill led with 7.5 points, followed by Kyla at 6.5, GFB at 5.9, and alwe at 5.3. Luna held 4.7 points, with other members including Ratna at 3.2, Hannah at 2.7, and others trailing further behind at 1.9 points.
Key discussion points:
The scoreboard served as a motivational and accountability tool for the group. The data was presented matter-of-factly, with no extended discussion on individual scores, but it set the tone for the session by reminding members of the importance of consistent participation and quality contributions. The emotional landscape chart was also briefly referenced, showing that 59% of the group's emotional tone was positive and 41% was neutral — a generally healthy emotional climate for the program.
Insights or decisions:
A notable observation was raised regarding the quality and quantity of questions being asked during sessions. The data showed that the number of questions had dropped significantly even as membership grew, and many questions were repetitive across sessions. This was flagged as a concern, with a note that questions such as "What gave you that idea?" or "What did you learn?" would eventually limit a member's score, as the system rewards more substantive, original questions. Members were implicitly encouraged to develop more thoughtful, layered questions that build meaningfully on each other.
Questions addressed:
No direct questions were raised during this segment, but the data itself prompted implicit reflection on participation quality.
---
Mindfulness & Breathing Exercise
Following the scoreboard review, Kyla led the group through a structured breathing exercise as a mindfulness warm-up before the main session content. The exercise followed a box-breathing-style pattern, guiding participants through cycles of inhaling for five counts, holding for three counts, and exhaling for seven counts. The exercise was repeated four times in total, with Kyla counting aloud to guide the group.
Key discussion points:
The breathing exercise was a deliberate and structured component of the session, designed to help participants center themselves emotionally before engaging with the topic of emotional intelligence. Kyla delivered the exercise with calm, measured pacing, and the group appeared to follow along without disruption. The exercise lasted approximately two and a half minutes and concluded with Kyla thanking the group.
Insights or decisions:
The inclusion of a breathing exercise at the start of a session on emotional intelligence was a thoughtful and thematically aligned choice. It demonstrated a practical application of emotional regulation techniques — specifically, the use of controlled breathing to manage internal states — which directly connected to the content that followed in the guest speaker's presentation.
Questions addressed:
No questions were raised during this segment.
---
Guest Speaker Presentation: Emotional Intelligence through Hindu Philosophy and Martial Arts
The primary content segment of the session was delivered by guest speaker Putu, who presented his personal perspective on emotional intelligence by drawing from two philosophical frameworks: the Hindu concept of Tatuam Asi and the ethics of his martial arts practice.
Key discussion points:
Putu opened by framing emotional intelligence as the ability to manage one's emotions effectively, emphasizing that while emotions are natural and important, mismanaging them can cause harm both to oneself and to others. He introduced the Hindu philosophical concept of Tatuam Asi, which translates roughly to "You and I are the same," explaining that this principle holds that all human beings share the same divine essence — the soul — and therefore harming another person is equivalent to harming oneself. He argued that this philosophical understanding forms a powerful foundation for emotional regulation, because when one truly internalizes the idea that others are fundamentally the same as oneself, the impulse to act harmfully out of unchecked emotion is naturally diminished.
Putu then extended this framework to his martial arts philosophy, explaining that in his discipline, practitioners are trained not only to be technically proficient fighters but also to deeply respect their opponents. The goal in martial arts, he explained, is not to harm the opponent but to apply technique and strategy within the rules of the discipline. He drew a vivid contrast between controlled, rule-abiding martial arts and what he described as "animal fighting" — unregulated, emotionally driven aggression that breaks rules and causes serious harm. The ability to hold one's emotion during a fight, he argued, is what separates a skilled martial artist from someone merely acting on impulse.
Putu also recommended meditation as a practical daily tool for emotional regulation, sharing that he personally wakes at 4:00 AM each morning to meditate, which he credited as a key practice for maintaining emotional balance. He further suggested that talking to trusted friends or discussing problems openly is another effective method for managing complex emotions.
Insights or decisions:
The most significant insight from Putu's presentation was the integration of spiritual and philosophical frameworks into the practical understanding of emotional intelligence. Rather than presenting emotional intelligence as a purely psychological or professional skill, Putu grounded it in a deeply humanistic worldview — one that sees empathy, restraint, and respect as moral imperatives rooted in the recognition of shared humanity. His point that emotions must be used "in the right place, at the right time, and in the right way" resonated as a practical takeaway for the group.
Questions addressed:
Several substantive questions were raised during the Q&A segment following Putu's presentation. alwe asked about the tension between winning in martial arts and the principle of not harming one's opponent, to which Putu clarified that winning and respecting one's opponent are not mutually exclusive — the goal is to win through skill and rule-following, not through harmful aggression. Wiati raised a nuanced question about the challenge of expressing emotions authentically when others may misinterpret that expression, and Putu responded by emphasizing the importance of timing and context in emotional expression. Intan asked a question about the practical application of emotional intelligence, and Putu reiterated the two philosophical pillars — Tatuam Asi and martial arts ethics — as guiding frameworks. Kyla asked how one can manage complex emotions such as jealousy, shame, and frustration, and Putu responded that age, education, and experience all shape one's capacity to manage such emotions, while recommending meditation and trusted conversation as primary tools. Ratna asked two questions: one about the relationship between material concerns and emotional philosophy (to which Putu clarified that emotional intelligence operates at the level of feelings and soul, not material comparison), and another about practical techniques for controlling emotion in the moment, to which Putu advised pausing before reacting, taking a breath, and giving oneself time to think before responding.
---
Member Weekly Challenges: Emotional Intelligence in Practice
Following the guest speaker segment, three members — Kyla, Jfp (Jeffrey), and alwe — each presented their personal weekly challenges, which were themed around emotional intelligence and self-reflection.
Key discussion points:
Kyla presented a challenge in which she identified three emotions she experienced during the day — happiness, boredom, and shyness — and reflected on the situations that triggered each. She described happiness as arising from social interactions, favorite foods, and hobbies; boredom from unstructured time when her phone was unavailable; and shyness from being repeatedly called upon in a math tutoring session to answer questions on a topic she had not yet mastered. Kyla's reflection was thoughtful and personal, and she articulated a clear understanding of why identifying emotions is valuable — it enables one to respond wisely rather than react impulsively.
Jeffrey presented a challenge centered on a moment of frustration with a friend who had asked for homework help but was being dismissive and unresponsive. Jeffrey described the experience of feeling intense anger but choosing to pause, give himself time, and allow his thoughts to clarify before responding. He noted that even a brief pause significantly changed the quality of his response, enabling him to act from a place of calm rather than impulse — a direct application of the emotional regulation principles discussed by Putu.
alwe presented a challenge covering three emotional experiences: frustration upon waking up late and being told by his mother to "make up for it tomorrow," amusement while playing games with a friend, and annoyance when his laptop screen went black during use. alwe's presentation was lighter in tone and more anecdotal, but it demonstrated an awareness of the range of everyday emotions and their triggers.
Insights or decisions:
A particularly interesting exchange occurred during the Q&A for alwe's challenge, when Kyla challenged alwe's strategy of "ignoring" an emotion for 10–15 seconds, noting that repressing emotions is generally considered unhealthy. alwe clarified that he was not suppressing the emotion but rather redirecting his attention to give himself a moment of calm — a distinction that aligns more closely with healthy emotional regulation strategies. This exchange demonstrated genuine critical thinking and peer learning within the group.
Questions addressed:
Jfp asked Kyla how she thought emotional intelligence would benefit her in the future, and Kyla responded that it would help her maintain relationships and support her career by enabling her to understand and manage human emotions more effectively. alwe asked Kyla how she manages the three emotions she identified, and Kyla explained that happiness needs no management, boredom is addressed by engaging in productive activities, and shyness is managed by refocusing on the task at hand rather than the feeling itself. Kyla asked Jeffrey what kind of situation caused his frustration, and Jeffrey explained the context of his friend's dismissive behavior during a homework help session.
---
Interactive Riddle Activity
The final content segment of the session was an interactive riddle and visual puzzle activity facilitated by ELF. The activity involved a series of short video riddles and logic puzzles that required participants to observe images carefully and apply deductive reasoning to identify culprits, spot dangers, or explain unusual situations.
Key discussion points:
The riddles covered a variety of scenarios: identifying a poisoner at a dinner party based on visual clues (gloves), determining which suspect was left-handed based on how they wrote their name, identifying a poisoned meal in a haunted castle, spotting a fugitive who had dyed her hair to evade airport security, identifying a life-threatening bride based on a hidden poison jar, solving a mystery about how a woman poisoned her flatmate using only one side of a knife, determining who was being careless in a boat, assessing who was being irresponsible with animals, and understanding why an old lady mistook a fashionably dressed woman for a prison escapee.
Insights or decisions:
The activity was highly engaging and generated the most spontaneous, enthusiastic interaction of the entire session. Participants actively competed to identify answers, debated their reasoning, and celebrated correct answers. The activity served as an effective cognitive engagement tool and a welcome change of pace after the more structured content segments. ELF used the activity to encourage close observation and logical thinking, skills that are implicitly connected to the session's broader theme of emotional intelligence — specifically, the importance of pausing, observing carefully, and not jumping to conclusions.
Questions addressed:
No formal questions were raised during this segment, but the activity itself was structured as a series of questions for the group to answer collectively.
---
Program Updates and Administrative Announcements
The closing segment of the session was dedicated to program updates and role assignments for the coming week.
Key discussion points:
ELF announced that the next session would feature VIT presenting the session summary, and requested that Kyla help contact Sekar to complete the materials for the upcoming Chapter 24 session on Data Storytelling, with Dr. Mustika as the speaker. ELF also clarified that Kyla would be taking over management responsibilities for the next cycle, which included collecting member challenges and stories and uploading them to the Substack platform. There was some initial confusion about the scope of Kyla's responsibilities, which ELF worked to clarify by sharing the relevant planning sheet on screen.
Jeffrey and Kyla provided updates on the bootcamp, which is themed around "Daily Discoveries" and features three character archetypes: a curious questioner, a Spirit Observer who observes before reacting, and a storyteller who transforms experiences into narratives that can influence others. Jeffrey reminded participants that the bootcamp runs every Monday and Friday and encouraged members to join for additional points. Kyla noted that bootcamp participants had not yet uploaded their T-shirt challenge submissions to the Padlet and urged them to do so.
ELF also requested that alwe send the session summary as soon as possible, and provided guidance on what to include — primarily a written reflection on what alwe understood from Putu's presentation.
Insights or decisions:
The bootcamp's three-character framework — curious questioner, Spirit Observer, and storyteller — was presented as a structured learning model that directly reinforces the program's emphasis on curiosity, mindfulness, and reflective communication. This framework aligns well with the session's emotional intelligence theme and suggests a coherent pedagogical design across the program's activities.
---
SECTION 3 — CHAT BOX SUMMARY
No significant chat activity occurred during this meeting. All substantive interactions, questions, and discussions took place verbally during the live session. The transcript does not contain any meaningful chat box contributions that would warrant separate documentation.
---
SECTION 4 — QUESTIONS BY PARTICIPANT
alwe — Question to Guest Speaker Putu: Martial Arts and Emotional Restraint
During the Q&A segment following Putu's presentation, alwe raised a question that touched on an apparent tension within the martial arts philosophy Putu had described. alwe asked how it is possible to reconcile the competitive imperative to win in martial arts with the philosophical principle of not harming or disrespecting one's opponent. This was a genuinely thoughtful question that probed the practical application of the philosophical framework Putu had introduced, and it reflected alwe's engagement with the content rather than a surface-level response.
Putu responded by clarifying that winning and respecting one's opponent are not contradictory goals. He explained that the discipline of martial arts requires practitioners to win through the correct application of technique and strategy, strictly within the rules of the sport. When a fighter abandons emotional control and fights with unchecked aggression, the result is what Putu described as "animal fighting" — a breakdown of the sport's ethical and technical framework that can cause serious injury and rule violations. The ability to hold one's emotion, Putu argued, is precisely what enables a fighter to perform at their best, because clear thinking and controlled movement are only possible when the practitioner is not overwhelmed by anger or fear. This response effectively reframed emotional restraint not as a limitation on competitive performance but as a prerequisite for it.
---
Wiati — Question on Authentic Emotional Expression and Misinterpretation
Wiati raised a nuanced and philosophically rich question during the Q&A, asking about the challenge of authentic emotional expression in social contexts. Her question addressed a real tension in emotional intelligence discourse: while suppressing emotions entirely is unhealthy and counterproductive, expressing emotions openly can sometimes lead to misunderstanding, with others dismissing or misreading the expression as excessive or inappropriate. She asked Putu for his perspective on how to navigate this challenge.
Putu's response emphasized the critical importance of context, timing, and intentionality in emotional expression. He argued that emotions, when expressed skillfully, can serve as powerful tools for communication — helping others understand one's motivations, intentions, and boundaries. The key, he explained, is to use emotion purposefully and strategically, choosing the right moment and the right manner of expression so that the message is received as intended rather than misinterpreted. He framed this as using emotion "as a weapon" — not in an aggressive sense, but in the sense of a deliberate, well-aimed communicative act that achieves a specific purpose, such as making a community member aware of a mistake or clarifying one's position in a conflict.
---
Intan — Question on the Practical Application of Emotional Intelligence
Intan asked a question directed at Putu regarding the practical application of emotional intelligence, seeking to understand how the philosophical frameworks he had described translate into everyday behavior and decision-making. While the audio quality made it difficult to capture the exact wording of Intan's question, Putu's response indicated that she was asking about how to apply the principles of Tatuam Asi and martial arts ethics in real-life emotional situations.
Putu responded by reiterating the two foundational pillars of his framework: first, the recognition that all people share the same essential nature, which creates a natural disincentive to harm others; and second, the martial arts principle of not harming one's opponent, which translates in everyday life to the practice of restraint, respect, and rule-following in interpersonal interactions. He emphasized that managing emotion requires first understanding the situation fully — its background, context, and the intentions of those involved — before choosing how to respond. This situational awareness, combined with the philosophical grounding of Tatuam Asi, forms the practical toolkit for emotional intelligence as Putu understands it.
---
Kyla — Question on Managing Complex Emotions
Kyla asked one of the most substantive and practically relevant questions of the session, directing Putu's attention to the challenge of managing complex, difficult emotions such as jealousy, shame, and frustration. This question moved the discussion beyond the general principles Putu had outlined and pushed toward specific, actionable guidance for situations where emotional regulation is most challenging.
Putu's response was multi-layered. He acknowledged that the capacity to manage complex emotions is shaped by three key factors: age, education, and personal experience — suggesting that emotional intelligence is a developmental skill that deepens over time rather than a fixed trait. He then offered two primary practical recommendations: daily meditation, which he described as his own personal practice of waking at 4:00 AM each morning to meditate; and open conversation with trusted friends or confidants, which he suggested as a way to process and externalize complex emotional experiences. He also returned to the philosophical foundation of Tatuam Asi, arguing that when one truly internalizes the belief that all people share the same divine essence, the intensity of emotions like jealousy and resentment naturally diminishes, because harming others through unchecked emotion is understood as equivalent to harming oneself.
---
Kyla — Question to alwe: Emotional Repression vs. Regulation
During the Q&A following alwe's weekly challenge presentation, Kyla raised a critically important conceptual question that demonstrated her engagement with the session's content at a deeper level. After alwe described his strategy of "ignoring" a difficult emotion for 10–15 seconds until it passed, Kyla challenged this approach by noting that repressing emotions — which ignoring them could be interpreted as — is generally considered psychologically unhealthy. She referenced the earlier discussion with Putu as context for her concern, showing that she was actively connecting ideas across different segments of the session.
This question prompted alwe to clarify his approach, explaining that he was not suppressing the emotion but rather giving himself a brief moment of calm — a temporary redirection of attention — before returning to a normal emotional state. This distinction is meaningful in the context of emotional intelligence: healthy regulation involves acknowledging an emotion and choosing how to respond to it, rather than denying or burying it. The exchange was one of the most intellectually substantive peer interactions of the session and demonstrated genuine critical thinking on Kyla's part.
---
Ratna — Two Questions to Guest Speaker Putu
Ratna asked two questions during the Q&A segment. Her first question appeared to address the relationship between material concerns and the philosophical framework Putu had described, asking whether the principle of Tatuam Asi applies equally to material inequalities as it does to emotional and spiritual ones. Putu clarified that the philosophy operates at the level of soul, feelings, and emotion — not material possessions or wealth — and that comparing material circumstances is a fundamentally different exercise from recognizing shared humanity at the level of inner experience.
Ratna's second question was more practically oriented, asking directly what one can do to control emotion in a difficult moment. Putu offered a clear, actionable response: try not to react immediately, hold the response for a moment, think twice before speaking or acting, use breathing techniques to calm the nervous system, and allow time for the initial intensity of the emotion to subside before engaging. This advice closely mirrored the breathing exercise Kyla had led at the start of the session, creating a satisfying thematic coherence across the session's components.
---
Jfp (Jeffrey) — Question to Kyla: Emotional Intelligence and the Future
Jeffrey asked Kyla a forward-looking question during the Q&A for her weekly challenge, asking how she thought emotional intelligence would benefit her in the future. This question encouraged Kyla to articulate a personal vision for the relevance of the skill beyond the immediate context of the program.
Kyla responded thoughtfully, explaining that emotional intelligence would help her maintain and strengthen her relationships with others, support her professional development and career, and deepen her understanding of how human emotions function — including how to recognize, manage, and respond to them in herself and others. Her answer reflected a mature and holistic understanding of emotional intelligence as a life skill rather than merely an academic concept.

This was flagged as a concern, with a note that questions such as "What gave you that idea?" or "What did you learn?" would eventually limit a member's score, as the system rewards more substantive, original questions. Members were implicitly encouraged to develop more thoughtful, layered questions that build meaningfully on each other.
Questions addressed:
No direct questions were raised during this segment, but the data itself prompted implicit reflection on participation quality.
---
Mindfulness & Breathing Exercise
Following the scoreboard review, Kyla led the group through a structured breathing exercise as a mindfulness warm-up before the main session content. The exercise followed a box-breathing-style pattern, guiding participants through cycles of inhaling for five counts, holding for three counts, and exhaling for seven counts. The exercise was repeated four times in total, with Kyla counting aloud to guide the group.
Key discussion points:
The breathing exercise was a deliberate and structured component of the session, designed to help participants center themselves emotionally before engaging with the topic of emotional intelligence. Kyla delivered the exercise with calm, measured pacing, and the group appeared to follow along without disruption. The exercise lasted approximately two and a half minutes and concluded with Kyla thanking the group.
Insights or decisions:
The inclusion of a breathing exercise at the start of a session on emotional intelligence was a thoughtful and thematically aligned choice. It demonstrated a practical application of emotional regulation techniques — specifically, the use of controlled breathing to manage internal states — which directly connected to the content that followed in the guest speaker's presentation.
Questions addressed:
No questions were raised during this segment.
---
Guest Speaker Presentation: Emotional Intelligence through Hindu Philosophy and Martial Arts
The primary content segment of the session was delivered by guest speaker Putu, who presented his personal perspective on emotional intelligence by drawing from two philosophical frameworks: the Hindu concept of Tatuam Asi and the ethics of his martial arts practice.
Key discussion points:
Putu opened by framing emotional intelligence as the ability to manage one's emotions effectively, emphasizing that while emotions are natural and important, mismanaging them can cause harm both to oneself and to others. He introduced the Hindu philosophical concept of Tatuam Asi, which translates roughly to "You and I are the same," explaining that this principle holds that all human beings share the same divine essence — the soul — and therefore harming another person is equivalent to harming oneself. He argued that this philosophical understanding forms a powerful foundation for emotional regulation, because when one truly internalizes the idea that others are fundamentally the same as oneself, the impulse to act harmfully out of unchecked emotion is naturally diminished.
Putu then extended this framework to his martial arts philosophy, explaining that in his discipline, practitioners are trained not only to be technically proficient fighters but also to deeply respect their opponents. The goal in martial arts, he explained, is not to harm the opponent but to apply technique and strategy within the rules of the discipline. He drew a vivid contrast between controlled, rule-abiding martial arts and what he described as "animal fighting" — unregulated, emotionally driven aggression that breaks rules and causes serious harm. The ability to hold one's emotion during a fight, he argued, is what separates a skilled martial artist from someone merely acting on impulse.
Putu also recommended meditation as a practical daily tool for emotional regulation, sharing that he personally wakes at 4:00 AM each morning to meditate, which he credited as a key practice for maintaining emotional balance. He further suggested that talking to trusted friends or discussing problems openly is another effective method for managing complex emotions.
Insights or decisions:
The most significant insight from Putu's presentation was the integration of spiritual and philosophical frameworks into the practical understanding of emotional intelligence. Rather than presenting emotional intelligence as a purely psychological or professional skill, Putu grounded it in a deeply humanistic worldview — one that sees empathy, restraint, and respect as moral imperatives rooted in the recognition of shared humanity. His point that emotions must be used "in the right place, at the right time, and in the right way" resonated as a practical takeaway for the group.
Questions addressed:
Several substantive questions were raised during the Q&A segment following Putu's presentation. alwe asked about the tension between winning in martial arts and the principle of not harming one's opponent, to which Putu clarified that winning and respecting one's opponent are not mutually exclusive — the goal is to win through skill and rule-following, not through harmful aggression. Wiati raised a nuanced question about the challenge of expressing emotions authentically when others may misinterpret that expression, and Putu responded by emphasizing the importance of timing and context in emotional expression. Intan asked a question about the practical application of emotional intelligence, and Putu reiterated the two philosophical pillars — Tatuam Asi and martial arts ethics — as guiding frameworks. Kyla asked how one can manage complex emotions such as jealousy, shame, and frustration, and Putu responded that age, education, and experience all shape one's capacity to manage such emotions, while recommending meditation and trusted conversation as primary tools. Ratna asked two questions: one about the relationship between material concerns and emotional philosophy (to which Putu clarified that emotional intelligence operates at the level of feelings and soul, not material comparison), and another about practical techniques for controlling emotion in the moment, to which Putu advised pausing before reacting, taking a breath, and giving oneself time to think before responding.
---
Member Weekly Challenges: Emotional Intelligence in Practice
Following the guest speaker segment, three members — Kyla, Jfp (Jeffrey), and alwe — each presented their personal weekly challenges, which were themed around emotional intelligence and self-reflection.
Key discussion points:
Kyla presented a challenge in which she identified three emotions she experienced during the day — happiness, boredom, and shyness — and reflected on the situations that triggered each. She described happiness as arising from social interactions, favorite foods, and hobbies; boredom from unstructured time when her phone was unavailable; and shyness from being repeatedly called upon in a math tutoring session to answer questions on a topic she had not yet mastered. Kyla's reflection was thoughtful and personal, and she articulated a clear understanding of why identifying emotions is valuable — it enables one to respond wisely rather than react impulsively.
Jeffrey presented a challenge centered on a moment of frustration with a friend who had asked for homework help but was being dismissive and unresponsive. Jeffrey described the experience of feeling intense anger but choosing to pause, give himself time, and allow his thoughts to clarify before responding. He noted that even a brief pause significantly changed the quality of his response, enabling him to act from a place of calm rather than impulse — a direct application of the emotional regulation principles discussed by Putu.
alwe presented a challenge covering three emotional experiences: frustration upon waking up late and being told by his mother to "make up for it tomorrow," amusement while playing games with a friend, and annoyance when his laptop screen went black during use. alwe's presentation was lighter in tone and more anecdotal, but it demonstrated an awareness of the range of everyday emotions and their triggers.
Insights or decisions:
A particularly interesting exchange occurred during the Q&A for alwe's challenge, when Kyla challenged alwe's strategy of "ignoring" an emotion for 10–15 seconds, noting that repressing emotions is generally considered unhealthy. alwe clarified that he was not suppressing the emotion but rather redirecting his attention to give himself a moment of calm — a distinction that aligns more closely with healthy emotional regulation strategies. This exchange demonstrated genuine critical thinking and peer learning within the group.
Questions addressed:
Jfp asked Kyla how she thought emotional intelligence would benefit her in the future, and Kyla responded that it would help her maintain relationships and support her career by enabling her to understand and manage human emotions more effectively. alwe asked Kyla how she manages the three emotions she identified, and Kyla explained that happiness needs no management, boredom is addressed by engaging in productive activities, and shyness is managed by refocusing on the task at hand rather than the feeling itself. Kyla asked Jeffrey what kind of situation caused his frustration, and Jeffrey explained the context of his friend's dismissive behavior during a homework help session.
---
Interactive Riddle Activity
The final content segment of the session was an interactive riddle and visual puzzle activity facilitated by ELF. The activity involved a series of short video riddles and logic puzzles that required participants to observe images carefully and apply deductive reasoning to identify culprits, spot dangers, or explain unusual situations.
Key discussion points:
The riddles covered a variety of scenarios: identifying a poisoner at a dinner party based on visual clues (gloves), determining which suspect was left-handed based on how they wrote their name, identifying a poisoned meal in a haunted castle, spotting a fugitive who had dyed her hair to evade airport security, identifying a life-threatening bride based on a hidden poison jar, solving a mystery about how a woman poisoned her flatmate using only one side of a knife, determining who was being careless in a boat, assessing who was being irresponsible with animals, and understanding why an old lady mistook a fashionably dressed woman for a prison escapee.
Insights or decisions:
The activity was highly engaging and generated the most spontaneous, enthusiastic interaction of the entire session. Participants actively competed to identify answers, debated their reasoning, and celebrated correct answers. The activity served as an effective cognitive engagement tool and a welcome change of pace after the more structured content segments. ELF used the activity to encourage close observation and logical thinking, skills that are implicitly connected to the session's broader theme of emotional intelligence — specifically, the importance of pausing, observing carefully, and not jumping to conclusions.
Questions addressed:
No formal questions were raised during this segment, but the activity itself was structured as a series of questions for the group to answer collectively.
---
Program Updates and Administrative Announcements
The closing segment of the session was dedicated to program updates and role assignments for the coming week.
Key discussion points:
ELF announced that the next session would feature VIT presenting the session summary, and requested that Kyla help contact Sekar to complete the materials for the upcoming Chapter 24 session on Data Storytelling, with Dr. Mustika as the speaker. ELF also clarified that Kyla would be taking over management responsibilities for the next cycle, which included collecting member challenges and stories and uploading them to the Substack platform. There was some initial confusion about the scope of Kyla's responsibilities, which ELF worked to clarify by sharing the relevant planning sheet on screen.
Jeffrey and Kyla provided updates on the bootcamp, which is themed around "Daily Discoveries" and features three character archetypes: a curious questioner, a Spirit Observer who observes before reacting, and a storyteller who transforms experiences into narratives that can influence others. Jeffrey reminded participants that the bootcamp runs every Monday and Friday and encouraged members to join for additional points. Kyla noted that bootcamp participants had not yet uploaded their T-shirt challenge submissions to the Padlet and urged them to do so.
ELF also requested that alwe send the session summary as soon as possible, and provided guidance on what to include — primarily a written reflection on what alwe understood from Putu's presentation.
Insights or decisions:
The bootcamp's three-character framework — curious questioner, Spirit Observer, and storyteller — was presented as a structured learning model that directly reinforces the program's emphasis on curiosity, mindfulness, and reflective communication. This framework aligns well with the session's emotional intelligence theme and suggests a coherent pedagogical design across the program's activities.

Total Meeting Duration: 1 hour 24 minutes 47 seconds
Host / Facilitator: JFP (Jeffrey) — Singapore-based session host
